source_refs.note: Topic 14.4.6 with the Interesting Information box, printed page 309. The garbled printed equations are written out and the third step noted.

blocks.text: The decrease in the concentration of ozone in the stratosphere is called depletion of ozone, caused by organic compounds called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), which are gases or low-boiling liquids at room temperature used as aerosol propellants and refrigerants. CFCs diffuse into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet radiation breaks them down to give chlorine free radicals, which break down ozone: CFCl3 with UV gives CFCl2 + Cl.; Cl. + O3 gives ClO. + O2; ClO. + O gives Cl. + O2 (the print writes the last step with O2). The chlorine radical formed in the last step can attack another ozone molecule, so the second and third steps repeat many times: the decomposition of one CFC molecule can destroy up to 100,000 molecules of ozone. CFCs are also 100,000 times more effective than CO2 at trapping heat in the atmosphere.

blocks.prompt: Write a short note on CFCs and ozone-layer depletion (exercise Q.4i; MCQ II, VI).
blocks.explanation: CFCs, once common as refrigerants and aerosol propellants, are so unreactive that they survive to reach the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light breaks a C-Cl bond and releases a chlorine radical. The radical converts ozone to oxygen and is regenerated when the ClO radical meets an oxygen atom, so one chlorine atom destroys ozone molecules repeatedly, up to 100,000 per CFC molecule, thinning the layer that shields the surface from ultraviolet.

items: CFCs (propellants, refrigerants) reach the stratosphere; UV frees Cl. radicals; Cl. + O3 gives ClO. + O2 and ClO. + O gives Cl. + O2, repeating: one CFC molecule can destroy 100,000 ozone molecules; also powerful greenhouse gases.
